answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a way of measuring directional information flow between two variables — in this context, between two neurons. Where mutual information just tells you how related two neurons' activity patterns are overall, transfer entropy asks a more specific, time-directed question: does knowing the past activity of one neuron help predict the future activity of another neuron, above and beyond what that second neuron's own past already tells you?

The passage introduces it alongside mutual information as one of the two basic tools for tracking how activity moves through a neural circuit. The article gives its formal definition and interpretation a bit further on: it measures how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on that second neuron's own past, and is read as the transfer entropy from one neuron's past to the other's future. Crucially, the source variable's past reduces uncertainty about the target's future after accounting for information already disclosed by the target's own past (autocorrelation).

The reason this distinction matters for the rest of the piece is spelled out just before: mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, whereas transfer entropy measures effective connectivity, meaning it captures something closer to actual information propagation rather than mere statistical association. This is why transfer entropy becomes the workhorse measure later in the article for building "effective networks" out of spike recordings, identifying which neurons feed into which, before the more elaborate partial information decomposition machinery is applied on top of those networks.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This sentence is introducing the two specific measurement tools the article is about to define, right after setting up the problem: given one neuron sending information and another receiving it, how do you track information moving through the circuit? The next two blocks of the article spell out exactly what each tool does, so this line is essentially a table of contents for what follows rather than a claim to unpack on its own.

Mutual information and transfer entropy are two long-standing measures from classical information theory (predating the multivariate decomposition the paper is centrally about). Mutual information, as the article goes on to explain, measures how our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes, depending on whether we are accounting for shared dependencies with Y, and can be thought of as a kind of nonlinear correlation between two neurons' activity, but it doesn't capture directionality or timing. Transfer entropy, by contrast, is built to capture that directional, time-ordered sense of "flow": it is described as measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on the target's own past. The article later frames this distinction as mutual information giving a measure of functional connectivity, while transfer entropy gives a measure of effective connectivity — i.e., actual information propagation rather than mere statistical association.

So the selected sentence is a pivot point: it closes the general framing of "information theory can be used to study neural circuits" and opens the concrete toolkit, with each tool's formal definition and citation number ([10] and [11]) pointing to the original sources in the reference list, which immediately follow in the text.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this article, transfer entropy is a measure of how much the past activity of one neuron reduces uncertainty about the future activity of another neuron, once that second neuron's own past (its autocorrelation) has been accounted for. The article gives the formal definition as the transfer entropy from X's past to Y's future, quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable's own past (autocorrelation) [spya-p4pyuy]. The article also notes a technical nuance: Xp does not necessarily have to be a single moment or bin but can be a multi-dimensional and potentially non-uniform embedding [spya-p4pyuy].

The article draws a sharp contrast between this and plain mutual information, which only measures an undirected, instantaneous statistical dependency and does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow" [spya-f6sbgx]. Transfer entropy fixes that: whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity. In other words, transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation [spya-p4pyuy]. There's also a side note that in the special case of binary signals it can be adapted further: in the special case of binary signals the TE can be modified to also provide a measure of excitation/inhibition balance using the sorted local transfer entropy [spya-p4pyuy].

Why it matters to the argument: the whole piece is building toward partial information decomposition (PID) as a way to study neural "computation," and transfer entropy is positioned as necessary but insufficient groundwork for that. The article states that information transfer captures the overall "flow" of information through the system; however, it is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information "interact" and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources [spya-s0db2g]. That limitation is exactly the gap PID is introduced to fill — transfer entropy tells you information moves from source to target, but not whether two sources are integrated redundantly or synergistically, which is the paper's central topic. This is made explicit in the two-neuron setup: Information transfer (discussed above) tells us about how the past of either source Xi informs the future of Y, but to understand "processing", we are interested in how the interaction between the two source variables' past influences the target's future in a way that is not reducible to either source considered individually [spya-wer4cd].

Transfer entropy also does empirical work later in the article, not just conceptual work: it's the tool used to build the "effective networks" from spike recordings on which PID is then run triad by triad, and the amount of transfer entropy in a triad turns out to reliably predict how much synergy that triad exhibits, as described in the sections on rich clubs and feedforward/recurrent connections [spya-kqkb58 spya-sw5ukx]. My inference is that this dual role — first as a motivating contrast (what transfer entropy can't tell you) and later as a working ingredient (what feeds into the PID triads) — is why the article introduces it so early, in Section 2, well before PID itself is defined.

"Synergistic" here names one of the three basic ways that multiple neurons' activity can relate to a target neuron's activity, the other two being redundant and unique. The article's abstract flags it as the mode the authors care about most: synergistic dynamics that quantifies the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source.

The intuition, spelled out later in the piece, is about what you can learn by watching two input neurons together versus watching each one separately. If knowing both neurons' states jointly tells you more about the target neuron's future than the two neurons could tell you added up separately, that extra, joint-only information is synergy: if the left-hand side (the "whole") is greater than the right-hand side (the sum of the "parts"), then there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In that case the target neuron is doing something like a genuine computation on its inputs together, rather than just reacting to each one independently — which is why the authors treat synergy as their working stand-in for "information processing" in a circuit.

The abstract is previewing a finding that runs through the rest of the paper: synergy isn't scattered randomly through neural circuits but turns up more in certain structural positions — emerging disproportionately in neuronal rich clubs, downstream of recurrent connectivity, and in the convergence of correlated activity. So this word is doing double duty here: it's introducing a technical concept the paper will formally define a few sections later, and it's flagging the specific empirical thread (synergy's relationship to network structure) that the rest of the article is built around.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the three outputs that partial information decomposition (PID) produces when applied to a set of neurons, and it's worth unpacking what each of the three terms means, since the rest of the abstract and the paper build directly on them.

The setup is: you have a target neuron and two (or more) source neurons feeding into it, and you want to know how the sources' activity relates to the target's activity. PID splits that relationship into three parts. As the article later explains, "Red(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that could be learned by observing X₁ or X₂, Unq(Xᵢ;Y) is the information about Y that could only be learned by observing Xᵢ, and Syn(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together." In plain terms: redundant information is what any one source alone would already tell you; unique information is what only one particular source can tell you (the other source doesn't have it); and synergistic information is what you can only see by looking at both sources' patterns together — neither source alone, examined separately, reveals it.

The reason the paper singles out synergy as the interesting one is explained just after this sentence: we focus particularly on the synergistic mode, which quantifies the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source. The idea is that synergy is the signature of actual computation or integration happening at the target neuron — the neuron isn't just adding up separate signals, it's doing something with the combination that neither input could produce on its own. That's the concept the whole review is built around: showing where in the brain this synergistic "computation" shows up and what it correlates with.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" information is the portion of what a target neuron's activity reveals about its inputs that cannot be found by looking at any single input alone — it only shows up when you consider the sources jointly. The article defines it formally through the two-neuron case: when the whole (joint mutual information from both source neurons) exceeds the sum of the parts (each neuron's individual mutual information with the target), that surplus is synergy, and the target is said to be performing "a kind of integrating 'computation' on all of its inputs considered jointly" [spya-e94ury]. In the formal partial information decomposition, synergy, Syn(X₁, X₂;Y), is defined as "the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together" [spya-h5jzvm], and Figure 1 depicts it as the region of total information not covered by either source's individual circle [spya-pjdgu6].

Synergy matters to the whole argument because the authors treat it as the signature of genuine information *processing*, as opposed to mere information *transfer*: ordinary tools like mutual information and transfer entropy can track how information flows between neurons, but they cannot say whether a neuron is doing something with that information beyond passing it along [spya-s0db2g]. The abstract frames synergy as the paper's central focus, describing it as the "higher-order" information carried by patterns of multiple inputs that is "not reducible to input from any single source" [spya-xn9j9k]. The empirical sections then use synergy as a lens for finding structure-function relationships — showing it is denser in network "rich clubs," rises with recurrent connectivity, and depends on how correlated converging inputs are [spya-fud8q3 spya-sd9fzd spya-hkhpex]. The summary makes the stakes explicit: the existence of synergy shows that neurons "do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total... but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli" [spya-rc5z33] — that is, synergy is the evidence that neurons compute rather than just accumulate.
